Giving thanks for victory (verses 1–6)

Happy are the people whose ruler places confidence in God's strength and finds joy in God's salvation.

Such a king takes pleasure in the advance of God's kingdom and trusts the Lord to sustain every effort made in its service.

All our blessings are gifts of God's goodness, not wages earned by our own worthiness.

Sometimes those blessings arrive earlier than expected, are greater than we imagined, or come before we even asked.

Sometimes God gives precisely what we had feared we would not receive.

In these circumstances we can say that he went ahead of us with his blessings.

Nothing can come before Christ himself.

But for humanity, no blessing has ever more wonderfully come before our request than redemption through Christ.

The Father has made the Son a universal and everlasting blessing to the world.

Through him the families of the earth have been and will be blessed.

Christ finds joy in the Father's favor toward him and toward the work he has accomplished.

Henry sees the Spirit of prophecy moving here beyond what can be said of an earthly ruler into what belongs to Jesus Christ alone.

No merely human king is blessed forever, much less a blessing for the whole world forever.

Confidence in the Messiah's ultimate victory (verses 7–13)

The psalmist teaches us to look forward through faith, hope and prayer, considering what God will yet accomplish.

David's victories foreshadow the complete defeat of Christ's enemies.

Some people could have received Christ as the One who would rule and save them.

But they rejected him and fought against him.

If they continue in rebellion, the memory of that refusal will become a torment that does not end.

God works in sinners through his grace, making them willing to come, receiving them into his favor and rescuing them from coming judgment.

May he exalt himself in our hearts by almighty grace, destroying every stronghold of sin and Satan.

How great should our joy be when we see our Brother and Friend upon his throne and think of every blessing we may receive from him!

Yet Christ himself delights in his exaltation because he can now bestow happiness and glory upon sinners who have learned to love and trust him.

[Ps.21.1-Ps.21.6]
Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
Thanksgiving for victory. | (1-6) |
Confidence of further success. | (7-13) |
Verses 1-6
Happy the people whose king makes God's strength his confidence, and God's salvation his joy; who is pleased with all the advancements of God kingdom, and trusts God to support him in all he does for the service of it. All our blessings are blessings of goodness, and are owing, not to any merit of ours, but only to God's goodness. But when God's blessings come sooner, and prove richer than we imagine; when they are given before we prayed for them, before we were ready for them, nay, when we feared the contrary; then it may be truly said that he prevented, or went before us, with them. Nothing indeed prevented, or went before Christ, but to mankind never was any favour more preventing than our redemption by Christ. Thou hast made him to be a universal, everlasting blessing to the world, in whom the families of the earth are, and shall be blessed; and so thou hast made him exceeding glad with the countenance thou hast given to his undertaking, and to him in the prosecution of it. The Spirit of prophecy rises from what related to the king, to that which is peculiar to Christ; none other is blessed for ever, much less a blessing for ever.
[Ps.21.7-Ps.21.13]
Verses 7-13
The psalmist teaches to look forward with faith, and hope, and prayer upon what God would further do. The success with which God blessed David, was a type of the total overthrow of all Christ's enemies. Those who might have had Christ to rule and save them, but rejected him and fought against him, shall find the remembrance of it a worm that dies not. God makes sinners willing by his grace, receives them to his favour, and delivers them from the wrath to come. May he exalt himself, by his all-powerful grace, in our hearts, destroying all the strong-holds of sin and Satan. How great should be our joy and praise to behold our Brother and Friend upon the throne, and for all the blessings we may expect from him! yet he delights in his exalted state, as enabling him to confer happiness and glory on poor sinners, who are taught to love and trust in him.

The suffering of Christ and the complaint of abandonment (verses 1–10)

The Spirit of Christ, who spoke through the prophets, testified in this Psalm about Christ's sufferings and the glory that would follow.

The Psalm begins with a sorrowful complaint about God's apparent withdrawal.

It may also give language to believers crushed by grief and fear.

For a child of God, the felt loss of God's presence is more painful than any other suffering.

Even the anguish of that loss can show that spiritual life remains active, because the soul still longs for God.

Complaining, Why am I sick? Why am I poor?, can reveal dissatisfaction with the world and its comforts.

But crying, “Why have you forsaken me?”, reveals a heart whose happiness depends upon God's favor.

These words belong especially to Christ.

He spoke them upon the cross as he poured out his soul before God (Matthew 27:46).

Being truly human, Jesus naturally recoiled from such dreadful sorrows.

Yet his zeal and love prevailed.

In his deepest suffering Christ still declared the holiness of his heavenly Father.

Indeed, his suffering itself demonstrated that holiness and became reason for his people to praise God more than for all their other deliverances.

No one who has truly hoped in God has ultimately been ashamed of that hope.

No one who sincerely sought him has done so in vain.

The Psalm also describes the contempt and scorn of human beings.

The Savior expressed the humble and despised condition into which he had been brought.

The history of Christ's birth and suffering helps explain the prophecy.

Christ suffers and prays for deliverance (verses 11–21)

Here we see Christ suffering and Christ praying.

His example prepares us for suffering and teaches us to seek God within it.

Henry sees even the manner of Christ's death foretold, though crucifixion was not practiced by the Jews in the psalmist's time.

His hands and feet were pierced and nailed to the cursed tree.

His body was suspended in extreme pain and torment.

His natural strength gave way under the suffering and the divine wrath he bore.

Who can stand before God's anger?

The life of sinners had been forfeited.

The life of the Sacrifice therefore had to become their ransom.

Jesus was stripped of his clothes upon the cross so that he might clothe us in his righteousness.

These things happened as Scripture foretold, confirming that Christ was the true Messiah.

They should also deepen our love for him as the best of friends, who endured all this for us.

During his agony Jesus prayed earnestly.

He asked that the cup of suffering might pass from him.

When we cannot rejoice in God as the object of our song, let us still rest upon him as our strength.

When the feeling of spiritual delight is absent, we can still receive the support of his grace.

Christ prayed to be delivered from the wrath of God.

The Lord has delivered, continues delivering and will deliver.

We should meditate upon Christ's suffering and resurrection until we experience in our souls the power of his resurrection and fellowship in his sufferings.

Praise for redemption and the risen Savior (verses 22–31)

Now the Savior speaks as risen from the dead.

Christ himself used the opening words of the Psalm's lament upon the cross.

The opening words of its triumphant praise are expressly applied to him in Hebrews 2:12.

All true praise must ultimately return to the work of redemption.

The suffering of our Redeemer was accepted by the Father as a full satisfaction for sin.

Although he offered himself on behalf of sinful people, the Father did not reject that offering.

This deserves our continual thanksgiving.

Humble hearts renewed by grace can find complete satisfaction and happiness in Christ.

Those hungering and thirsting for his righteousness will not waste their labor on what cannot satisfy.

People who pray much will also give thanks much.

Those who turn to God will devote themselves carefully to worshiping him.

Every tongue should confess Jesus Christ as Lord.

People of every social condition—high and low, rich and poor, enslaved and free—meet in him.

Since we cannot preserve our own lives, it is wise to entrust our souls through obedient faith to Christ, who can save and keep them alive forever.

A generation will continue serving the Lord.

God will maintain a church in the world until the end of time.

He will regard those future believers as his own, just as he cared for previous generations.

They will proclaim his righteousness, not their own, as the foundation of their hope and source of their joy.

Redemption by Jesus Christ is God's own work.

Here we see the free love and compassion of the Father and the Lord Jesus toward sinful people—the source of all grace and consolation, the pattern for Christian conduct and a guide through the treatment believers can expect in this world.

Every humbling and saving lesson can be found here.

Let those who attempt to establish their own righteousness ask why God's beloved Son would have needed to suffer so terribly if human deeds could atone for sin.

Let those who claim Christ's name while despising God's law ask whether Jesus suffered in order to give them permission to disobey it.

Let careless sinners flee the coming wrath.

Let trembling souls entrust themselves to this merciful Redeemer.

And let distressed and tempted believers confidently expect that the Lord will bring a happy end to every trial.

Chapter 22
Chapter Outline
Complaints of discouragement. | (1-10) |
With prayer for deliverance. | (11-21) |
Praises for mercies and redemption. | (22-31) |
Verses 1-10
The Spirit of Christ, which was in the prophets, testifies in this psalm, clearly and fully, the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow. We have a sorrowful complaint of God's withdrawings. This may be applied to any child of God, pressed down, overwhelmed with grief and terror. Spiritual desertions are the saints' sorest afflictions; but even their complaint of these burdens is a sign of spiritual life, and spiritual senses exercised. To cry our, My God, why am I sick? why am I poor? savours of discontent and worldliness. But, "Why hast thou forsaken me?" is the language of a heart binding up its happiness in God's favour. This must be applied to Christ. In the first words of this complaint, he poured out his soul before God when he was upon the cross, [Matt.27.46] Mt 27:46. Being truly man, Christ felt a natural unwillingness to pass through such great sorrows, yet his zeal and love prevailed. Christ declared the holiness of God, his heavenly Father, in his sharpest sufferings; nay, declared them to be a proof of it, for which he would be continually praised by his Israel, more than for all other deliverances they received. Never any that hoped in thee, were made ashamed of their hope; never any that sought thee, sought thee in vain. Here is a complaint of the contempt and reproach of men. The Saviour here spoke of the abject state to which he was reduced. The history of Christ's sufferings, and of his birth, explains this prophecy.
[Ps.22.11-Ps.22.21]
Verses 11-21
In these verses we have Christ suffering, and Christ praying; by which we are directed to look for crosses, and to look up to God under them. The very manner of Christ's death is described, though not in use among the Jews. They pierced his hands and his feet, which were nailed to the accursed tree, and his whole body was left so to hang as to suffer the most severe pain and torture. His natural force failed, being wasted by the fire of Divine wrath preying upon his spirits. Who then can stand before God's anger? or who knows the power of it? The life of the sinner was forfeited, and the life of the Sacrifice must be the ransom for it. Our Lord Jesus was stripped, when he was crucified, that he might clothe us with the robe of his righteousness. Thus it was written, therefore thus it behoved Christ to suffer. Let all this confirm our faith in him as the true Messiah, and excite our love to him as the best of friends, who loved us, and suffered all this for us. Christ in his agony prayed, prayed earnestly, prayed that the cup might pass from him. When we cannot rejoice in God as our song, yet let us stay ourselves upon him as our strength; and take the comfort of spiritual supports, when we cannot have spiritual delights. He prays to be delivered from the Divine wrath. He that has delivered, doth deliver, and will do so. We should think upon the sufferings and resurrection of Christ, till we feel in our souls the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings.
[Ps.22.22-Ps.22.31]
Verses 22-31
The Saviour now speaks as risen from the dead. The first words of the complaint were used by Christ himself upon the cross; the first words of the triumph are expressly applied to him, [Heb.2.12] He 2:12. All our praises must refer to the work of redemption. The suffering of the Redeemer was graciously accepted as a full satisfaction for sin. Though it was offered for sinful men, the Father did not despise or abhor it for our sakes. This ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving. All humble, gracious souls should have a full satisfaction and happiness in him. Those that hunger and thirst after righteousness in Christ, shall not labour for that which satisfies not. Those that are much in praying, will be much in thanksgiving. Those that turn to God, will make conscience of worshipping before him. Let every tongue confess that he is Lord. High and low, rich and poor, bond and free, meet in Christ. Seeing we cannot keep alive our own souls, it is our wisdom, by obedient faith, to commit our souls to Christ, who is able to save and keep them alive for ever. A seed shall serve him. God will have a church in the world to the end of time. They shall be accounted to him for a generation; he will be the same to them that he was to those who went before them. His righteousness, and not any of their own, they shall declare to be the foundation of all their hopes, and the fountain of all their joys. Redemption by Christ is the Lord's own doing. Here we see the free love and compassion of God the Father, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, for us wretched sinners, as the source of all grace and consolation; the example we are to follow, the treatment as Christians we are to expect, and the conduct under it we are to adopt. Every lesson may here be learned that can profit the humbled soul. Let those who go about to establish their own righteousness inquire, why the beloved Son of God should thus suffer, if their own doings could atone for sin? Let the ungodly professor consider whether the Saviour thus honoured the Divine law, to purchase him the privilege of despising it. Let the careless take warning to flee from the wrath to come, and the trembling rest their hopes upon this merciful Redeemer. Let the tempted and distressed believer cheerfully expect a happy end of every trial.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Confidence in God's grace and care.

The Lord is my Shepherd

The words “The Lord is my shepherd” express a believer's confidence and satisfaction in the care of the great Shepherd of all, the Redeemer and Preserver of humanity.

It is a wonderful thing to have a shepherd—and to know that this shepherd is the Lord himself.

A peaceful flock of sheep in green fields, tended by a wise, watchful and loving shepherd, pictures believers brought back to the Shepherd of their souls.

The wealthiest person who lives only for sensual pleasure finds even abundant possessions a dry pasture.

A godly person with little money has green pasture when faith enables that person to recognize God's goodness in everything received.

God gives the heart quietness and contentment regardless of its circumstances.

When his appointed ordinances provide green pasture, we should not merely pass through them but remain and feed upon them.

The Holy Spirit's consolations are the still waters beside which God's saints are led. They flow from the Fountain of living water.

People who walk in the paths of righteousness enjoy this comfort. The path of duty is genuinely pleasant, because righteousness produces peace.

Yet no one can walk that path unless God leads them into it and continues leading them onward.

Discontent and distrust spring from unbelief and lead to unsteady conduct. Trust the Shepherd's care and listen to his voice.

The valley of the shadow of death may refer to the deepest suffering or the darkest work of Providence.

It also describes the death separating the flock still on earth from the flock already in heaven.

But the psalm's expression reduces our fear: it is only death's shadow. A serpent's shadow cannot sting; a sword's shadow cannot kill.

It is a deep, dark valley, but valleys may be fruitful, and even death can bring spiritual comfort to God's people.

We walk through the valley. Christ's sheep will not be lost there: they reach safety on the other side.

Death is a king of terrors, but not to those who belong to Christ.

As they die, God restrains their enemy, guides them with his rod and upholds them with his staff.

The gospel contains enough comfort for believers in death, and everlasting arms support them.

At the Lord's table, his people feed upon the provisions of his love.

Satan and wicked people cannot destroy their true comfort while they are anointed by the Holy Spirit and drink from the full cup of salvation.

Past experience teaches believers to expect divine goodness and mercy to follow them throughout life.

They resolve to seek happiness in serving God now and hope to enjoy his love forever in heaven.

The Lord can make any condition pleasant through his Spirit's anointing and the joy of his salvation.

But those who hope to enjoy the blessings of God's house must also remain attentive to its duties.
classic_reading:
[Ps.23.1]
Chapter 23
Confidence in God's grace and care.
--"The Lord is my shepherd." In these words, the believer is taught to express his satisfaction in the care of the great Pastor of the universe, the Redeemer and Preserver of men. With joy he reflects that he has a shepherd, and that shepherd is Jehovah. A flock of sheep, gentle and harmless, feeding in verdant pastures, under the care of a skilful, watchful, and tender shepherd, forms an emblem of believers brought back to the Shepherd of their souls. The greatest abundance is but a dry pasture to a wicked man, who relishes in it only what pleases the senses; but to a godly man, who by faith tastes the goodness of God in all his enjoyments, though he has but little of the world, it is a green pasture. The Lord gives quiet and contentment in the mind, whatever the lot is. Are we blessed with the green pastures of the ordinances, let us not think it enough to pass through them, but let us abide in them. The consolations of the Holy Spirit are the still waters by which the saints are led; the streams which flow from the Fountain of living waters. Those only are led by the still waters of comfort, who walk in the paths of righteousness. The way of duty is the truly pleasant way. The work of righteousness in peace. In these paths we cannot walk, unless. God lead us into them, and lead us on in them. Discontent and distrust proceed from unbelief; an unsteady walk is the consequence: let us then simply trust our Shepherd's care, and hearken to his voice. The valley of the shadow of death may denote the most severe and terrible affliction, or dark dispensation of providence, that the psalmist ever could come under. Between the part of the flock on earth and that which is gone to heaven, death lies like a dark valley that must be passed in going from one to the other. But even in this there are words which lessen the terror. It is but the shadow of death: the shadow of a serpent will not sting, nor the shadow of a sword kill. It is a valley, deep indeed, and dark, and miry; but valleys are often fruitful, and so is death itself fruitful of comforts to God's people. It is a walk through it: they shall not be lost in this valley, but get safe to the mountain on the other side. Death is a king of terrors, but not to the sheep of Christ. When they come to die, God will rebuke the enemy; he will guide them with his rod, and sustain them with his staff. There is enough in the gospel to comfort the saints when dying, and underneath them are the everlasting arms. The Lord's people feast at his table, upon the provisions of his love. Satan and wicked men are not able to destroy their comforts, while they are anointed with the Holy Spirit, and drink of the cup of salvation which is ever full. Past experience teaches believers to trust that the goodness and mercy of God will follow them all the days of their lives, and it is their desire and determination, to seek their happiness in the service of God here, and they hope to enjoy his love for ever in heaven. While here, the Lord can make any situation pleasant, by the anointing of his Spirit and the joys of his salvation. But those that would be satisfied with the blessings of his house, must keep close to the duties of it.

The kingdom and its people (verses 1–6)

We do not belong to ourselves. Our bodies and souls belong to God.

Even people who neither know him nor acknowledge their relationship to him still belong to him.

Anyone who understands that the soul will exist forever, after surveying all the earth and its possessions, will recognize that worldly things cannot satisfy it.

Such a person will begin to desire to approach God and ask: What must I do to live in the happy and holy place where God makes his people holy and happy?

Religion is worthless if it never becomes a matter of the heart.

Only Christ's blood can cleanse our sins, and only the Holy Spirit's washing can renew us in holiness.

Through this work we become God's people and receive blessing from the Lord and righteousness from the God of our salvation.

God will make those who truly belong to him happy, completely and forever.

When God grants righteousness, his intention is also salvation.

Those whom he prepares for heaven will reach heaven safely and find what their souls have been seeking.

The King of glory (verses 7–10)

The magnificent entrance described here first refers to the solemn arrival of the ark in the tent David prepared for it, or in Solomon's later temple.

Henry also applies it to Christ's ascension into heaven and the welcome he received there.

Our Redeemer found heaven's gates closed because of sin, but having made atonement by his own blood, he could demand entry with full authority.

The angels were commanded to worship him (Hebrews 1:6).

They ask in wonder who this King is, and the answer declares that he is mighty in battle, powerful to save his people and subdue his and their enemies.

The psalm may also be applied to Christ entering human hearts through his word and Spirit, making them his temples.

He stands at the door and knocks (Revelation 3:20).

The heart's gates should open to him as a property is delivered to its rightful owner.

The psalm can also point us toward his glorious second coming.

Lord, open the everlasting door of our souls by your grace. May we receive you now and belong wholly to you, and finally be numbered with your saints in glory.

Concerning the King of that kingdom. | (7-10) |
Verses 1-6
We ourselves are not our own; our bodies, our souls, are not. Even those of the children of men are God's, who know him not, nor own their relation to him. A soul that knows and considers its own nature, and that it must live for ever, when it has viewed the earth and the fulness thereof, will sit down unsatisfied. It will think of ascending toward God, and will ask, What shall I do, that I may abide in that happy, holy place, where he makes his people holy and happy? We make nothing of religion, if we do not make heart-work of it. We can only be cleansed from our sins, and renewed unto holiness, by the blood of Christ and the washing of the Holy Ghost. Thus we become his people; thus we receive blessing from the Lord, and righteousness from the God of our salvation. God's peculiar people shall be made truly and for ever happy. Where God gives righteousness, he designs salvation. Those that are made meet for heaven, shall be brought safe to heaven, and will find what they have been seeking.
[Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10]
Verses 7-10
The splendid entry here described, refers to the solemn bringing in of the ark into the tent David pitched for it, or the temple Solomon built for it. We may also apply it to the ascension of Christ into heaven, and the welcome given to him there. Our Redeemer found the gates of heaven shut, but having by his blood made atonement for sin, as one having authority, he demanded entrance. The angels were to worship him, [Heb.1.6] He 1:6: they ask with wonder, Who is he? It is answered, that he is strong and mighty; mighty in battle to save his people, and to subdue his and their enemies. We may apply it to Christ's entrance into the souls of men by his word and Spirit, that they may be his temples. Behold, he stands at the door, and knocks, Rev 3:20. The gates and doors of the heart are to be opened to him, as possession is delivered to the rightful owner. We may apply it to his second coming with glorious power. Lord, open the everlasting door of our souls by thy grace, that we may now receive thee, and be wholly thine; and that, at length, we may be numbered with thy saints in glory.

Confidence in prayer (verses 1–7)

When we worship God, we should lift our souls toward him.

Anyone who waits upon God with faith and hopes in him with confidence will never have reason to be ashamed of that trust.

Even the most mature believer still needs and desires God's instruction.

If we sincerely want to know our duty and are determined to do it, we can trust the Lord to guide us.

David was especially eager for forgiveness.

When God pardons sin, Scripture says that he remembers it no more. This describes complete remission.

Our claim upon forgiveness and every needed good must rest on God's goodness, not ours; on his mercy, not our merit.

We should make that appeal while recognizing our unworthiness and trusting the riches of grace.

How vast is the mercy that can cover forever the sins and follies of a youth lived without God and without hope!

Blessed be the Lord: the blood of the great Sacrifice can cleanse every stain.

God guides and forgives sinners (verses 8–14)

We are all sinners, and Christ came into the world to save sinners, teach them and call them to repentance.

We judge the reliability of a promise by the character of the One making it. That is why we can depend on God's promises.

All the Lord's paths—his promises and providential dealings—are mercy and truth.

Through every circumstance, even severe affliction, his people may discover his mercy and the fulfillment of his word.

When they reach the end of their journey, they will understand more clearly that every path was merciful and true.

Humble people distrust themselves, want to be instructed and seek divine guidance.

God directs them by the written word, enabling them to find rest for their souls in the Savior.

Even when the body is sick and hurting, the soul may remain at peace in God.

Help during suffering (verses 15–22)

David ended as he began: looking to God and expressing his dependence and longing.

It is good to hope and wait quietly for the Lord's salvation.

If God turns toward us in favor, it matters little who turns away.

David appealed to the integrity of his dealings with his enemies.

He remained a sinner before God, but his conscience testified that he had not wronged those accusing him.

The Lord would finally give Israel rest from its enemies.

In heaven, God's people will be perfectly redeemed from every trouble.

Blessed Savior, you have graciously taught us that without you we can do nothing.

Teach us how to pray, how to approach you in your appointed way and how to lift our whole hearts and desires toward you, for you are the Lord our righteousness.
classic_reading:
[Ps.25.1-Ps.25.7]
Chapter 25
Chapter Outline
Confidence in prayer. | (1-7) |
Prayer for remission of sins. | (8-14) |
For help in affliction. | (15-22) |
Verses 1-7
In worshipping God, we must lift up our souls to him. It is certain that none who, by a believing attendance, wait on God, and, by a believing hope, wait for him, shall be ashamed of it. The most advanced believer both needs and desires to be taught of God. If we sincerely desire to know our duty, with resolution to do it, we may be sure that God will direct us in it. The psalmist is earnest for the pardon of his sins. When God pardons sin, he is said to remember it no more, which denotes full remission. It is God's goodness, and not ours, his mercy, and not our merit, that must be our plea for the pardon of sin, and all the good we need. This plea we must rely upon, feeling our own unworthiness, and satisfied of the riches of God's mercy and grace. How boundless is that mercy which covers for ever the sins and follies of a youth spent without God and without hope! Blessed be the Lord, the blood of the great Sacrifice can wash away every stain.
[Ps.25.8-Ps.25.14]
Verses 8-14
We are all sinners; and Christ came into the world to save sinners, to teach sinners, to call sinners to repentance. We value a promise by the character of him that makes it; we therefore depend upon God's promises. All the paths of the Lord, that is, all his promises and all his providences, are mercy and truth. In all God's dealings his people may see his mercy displayed, and his word fulfilled, whatever afflictions they are now exercised with. All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth; and so it will appear when they come to their journey's end. Those that are humble, that distrust themselves, and desire to be taught and to follow Divine guidance, these he will guide in judgment, that is, by the rule of the written word, to find rest for their souls in the Saviour. Even when the body is sick, and in pain, the soul may be at ease in God.
[Ps.25.15-Ps.25.22]
Verses 15-22
The psalmist concludes, as he began, with expressing dependence upon God, and desire toward him. It is good thus to hope, and quietly to wait for the salvation of the Lord. And if God turns to us, no matter who turns from us. He pleads his own integrity. Though guilty before God, yet, as to his enemies, he had the testimony of conscience that he had done them no wrong. God would, at length, give Israel rest from all their enemies round about. In heaven, God's Israel will be perfectly redeemed from all troubles. Blessed Saviour, thou hast graciously taught us that without thee we can do nothing. Do thou teach us how to pray, how to appear before thee in the way which thou shalt choose, and how to lift up our whole hearts and desires after thee, for thou art the Lord our righteousness.

modern_osis:
Original heading

David, in this psalm, appeals to God touching his integrity.

Integrity through grace

Under the Spirit of prophecy, David speaks of himself in a way that also makes him a type of Christ.

The claim of complete and spotless innocence is fully and uniquely true of Christ. It is through him that we are made complete.

Someone who walks sincerely while trusting wholly in God's grace is accepted according to the covenant mediated by Jesus, on the basis of Christ's perfect obedience even to death.

Such a believer asks God to examine and test the innermost soul.

Recognizing how deceitful the heart can be, the person seeks to discover and put to death every sin, to know whether faith is genuine and to obey God's holy commands.

Carefully avoiding evil company is both evidence of integrity and an important means of keeping it.

Hypocrites can attend God's appointed worship, so attendance alone cannot prove sincerity.

But coming in repentance, conscientious obedience and genuine devotion is a good sign of integrity.

David felt secure in God's grace. He delighted in blessing the Lord among congregations on earth and hoped soon to join the great assembly in heaven, praising God and the Lamb forever.

David, in this psalm, appeals to God touching his integrity.
--David here, by the Spirit of prophecy, speaks of himself as a type of Christ, of whom what he here says of his spotless innocence was fully and eminently true, and of Christ only, and to Him we may apply it. We are complete in him. The man that walks in his integrity, yet trusting wholly in the grace of God, is in a state of acceptance, according to the covenant of which Jesus was the Mediator, in virtue of his spotless obedience even unto death. This man desires to have his inmost soul searched and proved by the Lord. He is aware of the deceitfulness of his own heart; he desires to detect and mortify every sin; and he longs to be satisfied of his being a true believer, and to practise the holy commands of God. Great care to avoid bad company, is both a good evidence of our integrity, and a good means to keep us in it. Hypocrites and dissemblers may be found attending on God's ordinances; but it is a good sign of sincerity, if we attend upon them, as the psalmist here tells us he did, in the exercise of repentance and conscientious obedience. He feels his ground firm under him; and, as he delights in blessing the Lord with his congregations on earth, he trusts that shortly he shall join the great assembly in heaven, in singing praises to God and to the Lamb for evermore.

The Lord as light and strength (verses 1–6)

The Lord is the believer's light and the strength of that person's life.

We live and move not merely through him but in him.

His gracious presence, power, promises, readiness to hear prayer and the Spirit's witness within believers form the secret shelter of his tabernacle.

There his people find holy confidence and inward peace.

David longed for continual fellowship with God through his appointed ordinances.

All God's children desire to live in their Father's house.

They do not want merely to visit it like travelers spending one night, nor remain temporarily like servants who must eventually depart.

They want to dwell there all their days, as children belonging to their father.

If we expect praising God to fill our eternity, should it not also occupy our present lives?

However a Christian's earthly circumstances may differ, the favor and service of God remain the one necessary thing.

The believer seeks it, prays for it and rejoices in it.

Seeking God's face (verses 7–14)

Wherever a believer may be, there is a path through prayer to the throne of grace.

God calls us through his Spirit, his word and worship, and through particular events—both merciful and difficult.

When we foolishly pursue false and worthless things, he graciously calls us to seek our true happiness in him.

The invitation “Seek my face” goes out generally, but each of us must answer personally: “I will seek your face.”

The word is not useful to us until we receive its instruction.

Grace makes hearts willing to answer God's gracious call.

David asked for the Lord's favor, continuing presence, guidance and protection.

God's help often comes when every human helper has failed.

He is a more reliable Friend than even the most devoted earthly parents could ever be.

David believed he would see the goodness of the Lord.

The hope of everlasting life, together with foretastes of its glory and pleasures, is a powerful defense against fainting in trouble.

Meanwhile the Lord gives strength to bear present burdens.

Let us look to the suffering Savior, pray in faith and encourage one another to wait for the Lord with patience and earnest prayer.

Verses 1-6
The Lord, who is the believer's light, is the strength of his life; not only by whom, but in whom he lives and moves. In God let us strengthen ourselves. The gracious presence of God, his power, his promise, his readiness to hear prayer, the witness of his Spirit in the hearts of his people; these are the secret of his tabernacle, and in these the saints find cause for that holy security and peace of mind in which they dwell at ease. The psalmist prays for constant communion with God in holy ordinances. All God's children desire to dwell in their Father's house. Not to sojourn there as a wayfaring man, to tarry but for a night; or to dwell there for a time only, as the servant that abides not in the house for ever; but to dwell there all the days of their life, as children with a father. Do we hope that the praising of God will be the blessedness of our eternity? Surely then we ought to make it the business of our time. This he had at heart more than any thing. Whatever the Christian is as to this life, he considers the favour and service of God as the one thing needful. This he desires, prays for and seeks after, and in it he rejoices.
[Ps.27.7-Ps.27.14]
Verses 7-14
Wherever the believer is, he can find a way to the throne of grace by prayer. God calls us by his Spirit, by his word, by his worship, and by special providences, merciful and afflicting. When we are foolishly making court to lying vanities, God is, in love to us, calling us to seek our own mercies in him. The call is general, "Seek ye my face;" but we must apply it to ourselves, "I will seek it." The word does us no good, when we do not ourselves accept the exhortation: a gracious heart readily answers to the call of a gracious God, being made willing in the day of his power. The psalmist requests the favour of the Lord; the continuance of his presence with him; the benefit of Divine guidance, and the benefit of Divine protection. God's time to help those that trust in him, is, when all other helpers fail. He is a surer and better Friend than earthly parents are, or can be. What was the belief which supported the psalmist? That he should see the goodness of the Lord. There is nothing like the believing hope of eternal life, the foresights of that glory, and foretastes of those pleasures, to keep us from fainting under all calamities. In the mean time he should be strengthened to bear up under his burdens. Let us look unto the suffering Saviour, and pray in faith, not to be delivered into the hands of our enemies. Let us encourage each other to wait on the Lord, with patient expectation, and fervent prayer.

Prayer in danger (verses 1–5)

David prayed earnestly in faith, trusting the Lord as the Rock on whom his hope rested.

Believers should continue praying until they receive some assurance that God has heard them.

David asked not to be numbered with wicked people.

He wanted deliverance from their traps and from the danger of being infected by their sins.

His request was that God would never allow him to adopt the deceitful and treacherous methods his enemies were using against him.

Even the best believers are conscious of how readily they may be drawn aside. We should therefore pray diligently for preserving grace.

Those careful not to share in wicked deeds have reason to hope they will escape the judgments pronounced upon them.

David spoke in verse 4 of God's righteous judgments against evildoers.

Henry is explicit that this was not the expression of revenge or uncontrolled passion.

It was a prophetic statement that God will judge everyone who persists in wrongdoing.

The Lord will call sinners to account not only for the harm they have done, but also for the evil they planned and attempted.

Disregarding God's works is a source of sin and ultimately of ruin.

Thanksgiving and intercession (verses 6–9)

When God answers prayer, we should bless him.

He is our strength, upholding us through every service and suffering.

A believing heart will eventually rejoice. We should expect joy and peace through faith, and give all the praise to God.

The saints rejoice not only in their own comfort but also in the blessings of others.

The more people share in sunlight—or in God's favorable presence—the less none of us receives.

David ended with a short but comprehensive prayer for God's people, who are his precious inheritance.

He asked God to save them, bless them with every good gift, and especially nourish their souls through his appointed ordinances.

He prayed that God would guide their conduct and direct events for their good, not merely for his present generation but for all who would follow.

Only in heaven will God's people be lifted up forever, never again to fall or be cast down.

Lord Jesus, save us from our sins. As the Son of Abraham, bless us with righteousness.

As the good Shepherd of the sheep, feed us, and as the Resurrection and the Life, lift us forever from the dust.

Verses 1-5
David is very earnest in prayer. Observe his faith in prayer; God is my rock, on whom I build my hope. Believers should not rest till they have received some token that their prayers are heard. He prays that he may not be numbered with the wicked. Save me from being entangled in the snares they have laid for me. Save me from being infected with their sins, and from doing as they do. Lord, never leave me to use such arts of deceit and treachery for my safety, as they use for my ruin. Believers dread the way of sinners; the best are sensible of the danger they are in of being drawn aside: we should all pray earnestly to God for his grace to keep us. Those who are careful not to partake with sinners in their sins, have reason to hope that they shall not receive their plagues. He speaks of the just judgments of the Lord on the workers of iniquity, ver. #(4). This is not the language of passion or revenge. It is a prophecy that there will certainly come a day, when God will punish every man who persists in his evil deeds. Sinners shall be reckoned with, not only for the mischief they have done, but for the mischief they designed, and did what they could to effect. Disregard of the works of the Lord, is the cause of the sin of sinners, and becomes the cause of their ruin.
[Ps.28.6-Ps.28.9]
Verses 6-9
Has God heard our supplications? Let us then bless his name. The Lord is my strength, to support me, and carry me on through all my services and sufferings. The heart that truly believes, shall in due time greatly rejoice: we are to expect joy and peace in believing. God shall have the praise of it: thus must we express our gratitude. The saints rejoice in others' comfort as well as their own: we have the less benefit from the light of the sun, nor from the light of God's countenance, for others' sharing therein. The psalmist concludes with a short, but comprehensive prayer. God's people are his inheritance, and precious in his eyes. He prays that God would save them; that he would bless them with all good, especially the plenty of his ordinances, which are food to the soul. And direct their actions and overrule their affairs for good. Also, lift them up for ever; not only those of that age, but his people in every age to come; lift them up as high as heaven. There, and there only, will saints be lifted up for ever, never more to sink, or be depressed. Save us, Lord Jesus, from our sins; bless us, thou Son of Abraham, with the blessing of righteousness; feed us, thou good Shepherd of the sheep, and lift us up for ever from the dust, O thou, who art the Resurrection and the Life.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Exhortation to give glory to God.

The glory and power of the Lord

The powerful and honored people of this world are especially obligated to worship God and give him glory.

Yet few approach him in the beauty of holiness.

When we come to God through the Redeemer of sinners in repentance, faith and love, he accepts our imperfect service, pardons the sin still mixed with it and approves the holiness the Holy Spirit has enabled us to exercise.

This is the nature of true worship: giving the Lord the glory due to his name.

Every act of worship should be holy, devoted to God, his will and his glory.

Holiness is beautiful and gives beauty to everything done in worship.

David also described the Lord's power in the natural world.

Thunder, lightning and storms testify to his glory. We should respond by thinking highly of God's greatness and worshiping him with reverence.

The brilliance of lightning matches the terror of thunder.

These displays remind us both of God's power and of human weakness.

They also warn of how defenseless unrepentant sinners will be at the final judgment.

Yet the work of God's word upon human souls through the Holy Spirit is more extraordinary than any thunderstorm.

The proudest are humbled, stubborn hearts tremble, hidden thoughts are revealed, sinners are converted, and people once cruel, sensual and corrupt become gentle and pure.

If we have heard God's voice and fled to the hope he offers, we need not fear our Father's voice even when he speaks in judgment against his enemies.

Those who remain without shelter may tremble, but people who have entered his appointed refuge can thank him for their security.

They may look toward judgment without terror, as Noah was secure in the ark.

[Ps.29.1]
Chapter 29
Exhortation to give glory to God.
--The mighty and honourable of the earth are especially bound to honour and worship him; but, alas, few attempt to worship him in the beauty of holiness. When we come before him as the Redeemer of sinners, in repentance faith, and love, he will accept our defective services, pardon the sin that cleaves to them, and approve of that measure of holiness which the Holy Spirit enables us to exercise. We have here the nature of religious worship; it is giving to the Lord the glory due to his name. We must be holy in all our religious services, devoted to God, and to his will and glory. There is a beauty in holiness, and that puts beauty upon all acts of worship. The psalmist here sets forth God's dominion in the kingdom of nature. In the thunder, and lightning, and storm, we may see and hear his glory. Let our hearts be thereby filled with great, and high, and honourable thoughts of God, in the holy adoring of whom, the power of godliness so much consists. O Lord our God, thou art very great! The power of the lightning equals the terror of the thunder. The fear caused by these effects of the Divine power, should remind us of the mighty power of God, of man's weakness, and of the defenceless and desperate condition of the wicked in the day of judgment. But the effects of the Divine word upon the souls of men, under the power of the Holy Spirit, are far greater than those of thunder storms in the nature world. Thereby the stoutest are made to tremble, the proudest are cast down, the secrets of the heart are brought to light, sinners are converted, the savage, sensual, and unclean, become harmless, gentle, and pure. If we have heard God's voice, and have fled for refuge to the hope set before us, let us remember that children need not fear their Father's voice, when he speaks in anger to his enemies. While those tremble who are without shelter, let those who abide in his appointed refuge bless him for their security, looking forward to the day of judgment without dismay, safe as Noah in the ark.

Praise after deliverance (verses 1–5)

The great things the Lord has done for us through Providence and grace call us to grateful service.

We should do all we can to advance his kingdom, even though our greatest efforts are small.

The saints in heaven sing God's praises; why should not believers on earth sing to him too?

Of all God's attributes, none inspires more fear in the wicked or more comfort in godly people than his holiness.

It is a good sign that we share something of his holiness when we sincerely rejoice to remember it.

Our happiness rests upon God's favor.

If we possess that favor, we have enough, whatever else may be missing.

Yet while a believer feels God's displeasure, sorrow continues.

Learning from prosperity and trouble (verses 6–12)

When life goes well, we easily begin to imagine that it will always be so.

Recognizing our mistake should make us ashamed of carnal self-confidence.

If God hides his face, a faithful person may be distressed even without any other suffering.

But if God turns away for wise and just reasons, it would be foolish for us to turn away from him.

Instead, learn to pray in the dark.

A sanctified soul that returns to God will praise him forever.

The body that has become dust cannot perform the earthly service of God's house: the grave is a place of silence and no further earthly labor.

We rightly ask to remain alive when we want our lives to be devoted to God's praise.

In due time the Lord delivered David.

The tongue is our glory, and it is never better used than when blessing him.

David intended to continue praising God until he entered the place where praise would become his everlasting work.

Yet everyone must beware complacency during prosperity.

Neither external success nor inward comfort is permanently secure in this life.

God's favor grounds a believer's safety as firmly as a deep-rooted mountain, but temptations and trials still come.

If we become careless and sin, the Lord may hide his face; comfort fades and troubles return.

Let us therefore remain watchful, dependent upon his grace and constant in praise.

Verses 1-5
The great things the Lord has done for us, both by his providence and by his grace, bind us in gratitude to do all we can to advance his kingdom among men, though the most we can do is but little. God's saints in heaven sing to him; why should not those on earth do the same? Not one of all God's perfections carries in it more terror to the wicked, or more comfort to the godly, than his holiness. It is a good sign that we are in some measure partakers of his holiness, if we can heartily rejoice at the remembrance of it. Our happiness is bound up in the Divine favour; if we have that, we have enough, whatever else we want; but as long as God's anger continues, so long the saints' weeping continues.
[Ps.30.6-Ps.30.12]
Verses 6-12
When things are well with us, we are very apt to think that they will always be so. When we see our mistake, it becomes us to think with shame upon our carnal security as our folly. If God hide his face, a good man is troubled, though no other calamity befal him. But if God, in wisdom and justice, turn from us, it will be the greatest folly if we turn from him. No; let us learn to pray in the dark. The sanctified spirit, which returns to God, shall praise him, shall be still praising him; but the services of God's house cannot be performed by the dust; it cannot praise him; there is none of that device or working in the grave, for it is the land of silence. We ask aright for life, when we do so that we may live to praise him. In due time God delivered the psalmist out of his troubles. Our tongue is our glory, and never more so than when employed in praising God. He would persevere to the end in praise, hoping that he should shortly be where this would be the everlasting work. But let all beware of carnal security. Neither outward prosperity, nor inward peace, here, are sure and lasting. The Lord, in his favour, has fixed the believer's safety firm as the deep-rooted mountains, but he must expect to meet with temptations and afflictions. When we grow careless, we fall into sin, the Lord hides his face, our comforts droop, and troubles assail us.
